prompt: Sort each incident under the leg of the CIA triad it primarily attacks.
items: Attacker reads unencrypted traffic on public Wi-Fi
Botnet floods the public website with traffic
Customer database exfiltrated and posted online
Firmware replaced with a tampered build
Payroll figures silently altered in the database
Ransomware encrypts the file server
hints: Name the property the attacker destroyed, not the technology they used. The same technology shows up as a control on one side and a weapon on the other.

Ask what the attacker needed to happen for the attack to succeed: someone sees the data, the data changes, or its owner can't use it. Classify by that goal, even if other damage follows along the way.

prompt: Sort each measure under the property it primarily provides.
items: Collecting only the data fields the service actually needs
Digitally signing an approved payment so it traces to one named employee
Honouring a customer's request to erase what you hold about them
Keeping a tamper-evident audit log of who changed each record
Requiring a password plus a one-time code from the user's phone
Unlocking a workstation with a registered fingerprint
hints: Two of these properties involve identity, so check which job the measure does: verifying a person before they are allowed to act, or leaving evidence of an action that someone else could check later.
Ask whose interest the measure serves first: the organisation's need to know who is acting and what they did, or the individual's control over information about themselves.

prompt: Sort each control by its TYPE — how it does its job. Ignore when it acts; that is its function, not its type.
items: A firewall filtering inbound traffic by rule
A locked door on the server room
A perimeter fence around the data centre
An acceptable-use policy signed by every employee
Background checks run before a new hire starts
Full-disk encryption on every laptop
hints: Ask what actually does the enforcing: a machine, a rule that people follow, or a barrier in the physical world.

Imagine every person stopped following instructions tomorrow. Would the control keep working on its own? If it only works because people carry out a decision or a process, paperwork or not, that tells you its type.

prompt: Each situation is most directly about one canon's subject matter: public safety and the infrastructure (I), your own honesty and legality (II), what you owe the client who hired you (III), or the standing of the profession (IV). Sort them. Note that ranking settles conflicts of *duty* — it is not how you classify what a situation is about.
buckets: Canon I — protect society and the infrastructure
Canon II — act honourably, honestly, justly, responsibly and legally
Canon III — provide diligent and competent service to principals
Canon IV — advance and protect the profession
items: A vendor ignores your reports of a medical-device firmware flaw while patients remain at risk, and you keep pressing for a fix
You decline to exaggerate a threat in a sales pitch to frighten a prospect into buying
You refuse to scan a network you have no written authorisation to test
You report a peer who is selling leaked ISC2 exam questions to candidates
You report a vulnerability you found in a city's emergency dispatch system
You spend an afternoon each month mentoring junior analysts with no billable work attached
You tell a client up front that a specialised cloud engagement is beyond what you are qualified to deliver
You turn down a second client whose work would create a conflict of interest with your current engagement
hints: Test the duty, not the people who benefit: would you owe this even if nobody had hired you? If not, it is about your principals. If you would, decide whether it is about harm reaching the public, your own conduct, or the field as a whole.

Honesty runs through almost every situation here, so it won't separate the canons on its own. Ask which relationship the situation sits inside: an engagement you have taken on, the public at large, the profession's community, or simply how you yourself behave.

prompt: A new risk has just been raised: an internet-facing server is running unpatched software. Put the five steps of handling it in the order you would actually perform them.
items: Apply the control and verify it actually works
Assess likelihood x impact and rank it against the other risks
Choose a treatment: mitigate, transfer, avoid or accept
Document the residual risk and have it formally accepted
Identify the asset, the threats to it, and the vulnerabilities they could exploit
hints: For each step, ask what it needs as input before it can start, and which other step produces that input. Order them as a chain of dependencies, not by which sounds most important.
Separate deciding, doing and signing off — they are different steps. A sign-off is only honest once you know what the work actually achieved, not what it was meant to achieve.

prompt: Sort each document or statement into the governance layer it belongs to.
items: All production servers must run the approved hardened OS image
Data at rest must be encrypted with AES-256
Every system must have a named owner who is accountable for its security
HIPAA's requirements for safeguarding protected health information
Step 1: open the admin console. Step 2: select Enrol device. Step 3: scan the QR code
The organisation will protect the confidentiality of all customer data
To report a suspected phishing email, click Report, then forward it to the security inbox
Where practical, prefer a passphrase of four or more words
hints: Ask two separate questions of each item: is it binding or only advised, and how much does it specify — a goal or responsibility with no 'how', a named technology or setting, or a series of actions? Then check whether it comes from inside the organisation at all.
Mandatory does not mean specific. A rule can bind everyone and still name no product, setting or step, and naming exactly what to use is not the same as telling you how to do it.
